title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
hook: I set before you life and death: choose life

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna and the hunger that taught a lesson. Your line was not by bread alone. What were you hungry for, besides food? Day four hundred eight.

Most of the choices that shape a life don't feel like big choices. They feel like Tuesday. Whether to text back or let it slide. Whether to go to bed or watch one more. Whether to say the true thing or the easy one. Whether to get up and walk or stay on the couch. Each one is tiny. But laid end to end, they become a direction. Moses is at the end of his great speech in Deuteronomy. He's spent chapters laying out the way of life he hopes his people will walk. And now, at the very end, he boils it all down to a single choice, and he sets it in front of them like two plates on a table.
screen: `CHOICES THAT FEEL LIKE TUESDAY.` → `END TO END, A DIRECTION.` → `TWO PLATES ON A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Moses says it, in the King James Bible: "See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil." And a few verses on, he calls witnesses: "I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live." Choose life. Two words in English. In Hebrew it's even more compact: u-vacharta ba-chayyim. And chayyim, life, is a plural word in Hebrew, as if life were always more than one thing: breath and family and land and God, all at once. It's the same word in the Jewish toast, l'chaim, to life. Notice what Moses doesn't do. He doesn't choose for them. He sets it out, and he pleads. And just before this, he says something hopeful about how possible it is. This isn't too hard for you, he says, or far away. It isn't up in heaven, or across the sea. "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." The good life isn't a distant mountain to climb. It's as close as your own mouth. And then Moses says what life is: loving God, listening to his voice, holding on to him, "for he is thy life, and the length of thy days." Christians have heard echoes of this all through the New Testament, from Jesus' words about two roads, one narrow, to Paul quoting the word is nigh thee in his letter to the Romans. Life and death aren't only at the end. They're on the table every day.
screen: `LIFE AND GOOD, DEATH AND EVIL.` · `CHAYYIM: LIFE, ALWAYS PLURAL.` · `THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.` · `FOR HE IS THY LIFE.` · then, large: `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose the life-giving option once. Settle, and breathe. Think ahead through the rest of your day. Somewhere in it there's a small fork: two plates on the table. One option leaves you, or someone else, a little more alive. Water instead of the third coffee. A walk instead of the scroll. Calling your mother instead of putting it off. The kind answer instead of the clever one. Find that fork now, before it arrives. Picture yourself choosing life there. If you pray, you can ask for help to choose it. The bell holds the time.
Choose life. Moses' final plea in Deuteronomy: life and death are set before you, and the word is near, in your mouth and in your heart.
Your line: choose life. Today, when you reach that small fork you found, pick the plate that gives life, and say the line to yourself as you do. Day four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to Deuteronomy 30 when speaking about daily decisions and moral choices, and Paul quotes 'the word is nigh thee' from this chapter in Romans 10.

original.note: Hebrew: life. The word is plural in form, and gives the toast l'chaim, to life.

trapdoor: what it means: Moses' last plea to his people, setting life and death before them, and saying the good way is near, in their mouths and hearts.
what a scholar hears: u-vacharta ba-chayyim; chayyim is plural in form; and Deuteronomy 30:14 is quoted by Paul in Romans 10:8.

notes: 'Chayyim is plural, as if life were always more than one thing': the plural form is grammatical fact; the interpretation is offered lightly ('as if'). Confirm it doesn't read as a preacher's etymology.
Phrase 'choose life' has modern political uses; the script stays with the text. Keeper may wish to note this.
